A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same influence-function framework for diffusion-model attribution. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across substantial appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR attribution experiments, including LDS scores, counterfactual retraining, Hessian ablations, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds ArtBench and EK-FAC results, computational-cost measurements, and diffusion-loss correlation analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3.1.2 adds eigenvalue-corrected K-FAC, changing the curvature approximation used for attribution. The original K-FAC-expand pipeline, proxy measurements, quantisation, and query batching remain. Appendix F largely documents implementation and caching strategies rather than establishing changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CIFAR-10 and its CIFAR-2 subset; v3 extends evaluation beyond that underlying dataset to ArtBench for diffusion-loss attribution and computational costs (Figure 2a; Tables 2–5). ArtBench is not added to the ELBO or trajectory evaluations, and its precise data composition remains undocumented.

E2.justification: Figure 2a adds EK-FAC Influence as an evaluated comparison variant. TRAK, D-TRAK, CLIP similarity, and exact retraining remain in the corresponding LDS comparisons, while Figure 3 retains its original comparator set. Newly discussed related methods are not thereby evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New runtime comparisons specify one A100 GPU and 200 queries; ArtBench tables specify 125 Monte Carlo samples and a model with a pretrained component. Existing CIFAR protocol descriptions remain unchanged. Figure 3 doubles the plotted observations per method, but both experimental-details sections still specify five target samples, leaving the precise sampling revision unclear.

E4.justification: The central MC-Fisher versus empirical-Fisher and K-FAC-expand versus reduce ablation in v1 Figure 4 is removed, not relocated. v3 adds the K-FAC/EK-FAC comparison and diffusion-loss stability analysis in Figure 17. Earlier compression, damping, timestep, and down-weighting analyses are largely retained under new numbering.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeds for each of 100 LDS subsets and standard errors over generated samples in Figures 2 and 3. The reported uncertainty conventions remain unchanged; revised means and error-bar values do not establish a new statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 2a revises K-FAC loss LDS from 21.5% to 20.9% on CIFAR-2 and from 18.3% to 19.8% on CIFAR-10. New EK-FAC scores are 27.4%, 23.2%, and 16.9% on CIFAR-2, CIFAR-10, and ArtBench. On ArtBench, ordinary K-FAC scores 10.0%, below D-TRAK's 13.8%. Figure 3 values also change, and new cost and loss-correlation results accompany removal of the earlier Hessian-ablation results.

T1.justification: Appendices C and F.1 add formal K-FAC weight-sharing derivations and computational-complexity arguments. Equations (8) and (11) replace the identity/loss decomposition with log/exponentiated loss and revise the associated linearity condition. This is not a successful correction as written: the log map yields a negative outer product under the stated GGN definition. Appendix A's influence-function proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a unified, scalable influence-function framework, better attribution performance without method-specific tuning, and limitations in predicting numerical measurement changes. The added evidence does not meaningfully redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v1 interprets nearly constant ELBO values as evidence that ELBO may be a poor probability proxy. v3 instead suggests that sufficiently large training subsets can produce nearly identical learned distributions, qualifying Observation 3 accordingly. Appendix I adds interpretations of influence-magnitude overestimation and timestep-dependent stability. The earlier trajectory reparameterisation caveat and Hessian-ablation interpretation are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds implementation pseudocode, caching alternatives, hardware identification, model-parameter counts, stage runtimes, and memory requirements. This substantially expands implementation and resource transparency. Existing CIFAR settings and package links largely remain, while ArtBench preprocessing and training details are still missing.

R1.justification: New Appendix E substantially expands positioning within diffusion attribution, influence functions, and K-FAC/EK-FAC research. Added discussions include George et al., group-influence extensions, concurrent Lin et al. work, and Kadkhodaie et al.'s relevance to distribution stability. This goes beyond bibliographic updates to existing citations.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. Local edits correct language, promote the GGN background to Section 2.3, move evaluation definitions from Section 4 to Appendix D, and organise the expanded appendices. The revision does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is restructured with an ArtBench panel, an EK-FAC row, and revised axis ranges. The Hessian-ablation figure disappears, a diffusion-loss correlation figure is added, and Appendix F introduces five tables and two algorithm displays. Most remaining supplementary figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: ArtBench/EK-FAC evaluations and explicit runtime and memory reporting improve empirical breadth and make the central scalability claim more assessable. These gains are tempered by removal of the Hessian-choice ablation, incomplete ArtBench documentation, and unreconciled superiority wording: Figure 2a now places ordinary K-FAC below D-TRAK on ArtBench. The net improvement is therefore limited.
